findings.reason: The protected Python solution implements an in-memory SQL database class using a dictionary of tables mapping names to column counts, auto-incrementing next_id counters, and dictionary rows. The implementation provides ins, rmv, sel, and exp methods with validation. The design achieves expected O(1) ins/rmv/sel per operation and linear O(E) export; no candidate is required.

Row IDs increment monotonically and are never reused upon removal. Column index validation is 1-indexed, returning '<null>' for invalid cell/row lookups. Exports format surviving rows as CSV strings prefixed by row ID in creation order.

Operations ins, rmv, and sel run in expected O(1) time. Method exp runs in O(E) time where E is exported cell count. Total space is O(n + S) for n tables and S stored cells. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts operations and arguments lists, executing constructor and method calls according to expected signatures and returning the result list.

The approach accurately details dictionary-based schema separation, ID auto-increment validation, live-state query logic, and O(1) operation / O(E) export bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover dense row array overhead, linear table searches, failed insertions, deleted latest row behavior, invalid selections, and CSV export ordering.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical dictionary-based SQL class design with SHA-256 digests 81219fe130388d04cc8f37b580349d8bad87cd0825ec10400d07bea1cb01bd76 and 66fecbbcfd937e3f4328187e2ff93a383a5a94e84aa00182cf1b89c81bdcde9d. Verified submission remains untouched.
